summary: San Bernardino County is the largest county by area in the contiguous United States — over 20,000 square miles stretching from the eastern Los Angeles Basin suburbs all the way to the Nevada and Arizona borders, encompassing everything from 11,000-foot peaks in the San Bernardino Mountains to the stark emptiness of the Mojave Desert and Death Valley's doorstep. That scale creates a county of almost absurd internal variety: a population density of just 110 people per square mile belies the fact that most of the 2.2 million residents cluster in the southwestern corner, while vast eastern expanses hold virtually no one. The western cities function largely as a bedroom community for greater Los Angeles, with logistics and warehousing — anchored by massive distribution centers near the Ontario and San Bernardino rail and freeway corridors — ranking among the dominant local industries alongside healthcare systems like Loma Linda University Medical Center and military operations at Fort Irwin. A median home price of $475,000 against a median household income of $82,184 yields a price-to-income ratio around 5.8, meaningfully more accessible than neighboring Los Angeles or Orange counties, though median rent at $1,706 still claims a sizable share of that income. The climate data tells an unambiguous sun story — 10.5 hours of daily sunshine and average highs around 77°F — but altitude matters enormously here; a valley-floor subdivision and a cabin near Big Bear Lake or Lake Arrowhead might as well be in different states. With 636 schools, average ELA scores 28.6 points below standard and math scores 65.9 points below, the educational metrics lag state averages considerably. The county's essential tension is that its affordability and sheer space come packaged with long commutes, desert heat in the lowlands, and an infrastructure network built more for trucks and cars than for pedestrians — a place defined less by a single identity than by the distance between its many identities.
